title: Back then
job: Habits and states in the past; then against now
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: kāna AND ITS SISTERS are one grammatical class of four: kāna, mā zāla, aṣbaḥa and ṣāra. Each stands at the head of a sentence that would otherwise have no verb, or in front of a present-shaped verb, and each does the same structural thing. One shape, four meanings.
THE HABITUAL PAST is kāna plus a plain PRESENT verb: kuntu adrus, I used to study. The person is written twice, once on kāna and once on the verb behind it, and both must agree.

English marks the habitual past with used to and would. Arabic has neither: kāna alone carries it. Reaching for a past shape in the second slot — kuntu darastu — builds L4-M3's pluperfect instead, which means I HAD studied.
mā zāla, still, is the same frame with a different meaning: mā zāltu adrus, I still study. Its present-shaped twin lā yazāl says exactly the same thing and is commoner in writing.
aṣbaḥa and ṣāra mean became. They take a PREDICATE — an adjective or a noun — rather than a verb: aṣbaḥa al-jaww bārid, the weather turned cold.
The family's negative is lam yaʿud, no longer, and it needs no new machinery: L4-M6's lam with the jussive of yaʿūd. lam aʿud adrus, I no longer study.
English still and yet are a pair, and mā zāla has no yet inside it. The not-yet half is L4-M6's lam plus the jussive plus baʿd, and the two frames never meet.
THEN AGAINST NOW is built rather than taught: fī al-māḍī plus a kāna clause, then L4-M2's ammā al-ān fa- with a present verb. Keep it to two clauses — a three-part then/later/now is L5's.
tilka is the far demonstrative for a feminine noun or a non-human plural: tilka al-ayyām, those days. It is the phrase a past stretch of time gets told in.

sentences.display: kuntu adrus fī al-jāmiʿa kull yawm
sentences.script: كنت أدرس في الجامعة كل يوم
sentences.cue: I used to study at the university every day
sentences.literal: I-was I-study in the-university every day

words.note: The habitual past: L1-M5's kāna carries the pastness and the second verb stays in its plain present shape. L3-M10 used this frame once; here it is the grammar.

sentences.trap: English has two shapes for this — used to study, would study — and neither has an Arabic equivalent. kāna alone does the work, and the verb behind it does not move.
sentences.sound: KUN-tu AD-rus: two separate words, each with its own stress; nothing joins them.

variations.display: kāna yadrus fī al-jāmiʿa kull yawm
variations.script: كان يدرس في الجامعة كل يوم
variations.cue: He used to study at the university every day
variations.changed: the person — and it is written on BOTH verbs, kāna and yadrus

variations.display: kuntu adrus fī al-bayt kull yawm
variations.script: كنت أدرس في البيت كل يوم
variations.cue: I used to study at home every day
variations.changed: where the habit happened

mistake.why: A past verb in the second slot. That is L4-M3's pluperfect frame minus its qad, and it means I HAD studied — a different past, not a habit.

sentences.usage: Describing what your life used to look like.
sentences.mnemonic: kāna is the only word that goes back; the verb behind it stays home.

sentences.display: mā zāltu adrus al-ʿarabiyya kull yawm
sentences.script: ما زلت أدرس العربية كل يوم
sentences.cue: I still study Arabic every day
sentences.literal: Not I-ceased I-study the-Arabic every day

words.note: Still — literally I have not ceased. It is one of kāna's sisters and sits in exactly kāna's slot, in front of a plain present verb.

sentences.trap: English still is an adverb you drop in anywhere. Arabic still is a VERB at the head of the sentence, and the verb it governs stays present-shaped behind it.
sentences.sound: mā ZĀL-tu: the zāl is long in the middle, and the -tu is the same I-ending as in kuntu.

variations.display: mā zāla ṣadīqī yadrus al-ʿarabiyya
variations.script: ما زال صديقي يدرس العربية
variations.cue: My friend still studies Arabic
variations.changed: the third person — mā zāla, with the person on the sister verb

variations.display: mā zālat ummī fī al-bayt
variations.script: ما زالت أمي في البيت
variations.cue: My mother is still at home
variations.changed: a feminine subject, and no second verb at all — just a predicate

mistake.why: A past verb behind mā zāltu. The sisters all take a present-shaped verb; a past one here says nothing at all.

sentences.usage: Saying a habit has survived into the present.
sentences.mnemonic: mā zāltu = I have not stopped, so what follows is still going.

sentences.cue: I no longer study at the university

words.note: The family's negative, and no new machinery: L4-M6's lam with the jussive of yaʿūd, to return. Literally I did not go back to studying.

sentences.trap: English no longer is two adverbs. Arabic is a negated verb of returning with the real verb behind it, which is why nothing in the English sentence tells you where to put the negative.
sentences.sound: lam a-ʿUD: the ʿayn sits between the a and the u and squeezes them apart.

variations.display: lam yaʿud ṣadīqī yadrus fī al-jāmiʿa
variations.script: لم يعد صديقي يدرس في الجامعة
variations.cue: My friend no longer studies at the university
variations.changed: the third person, on the negated sister and not on the far verb

variations.display: lam aʿud adhhab ilā as-sūq kull yawm
variations.script: لم أعد أذهب إلى السوق كل يوم
variations.cue: I no longer go to the market every day
variations.changed: which habit stopped

mistake.display: mā zāltu lā adrus fī al-jāmiʿa
mistake.script: ما زلت لا أدرس في الجامعة
mistake.why: Still plus a negative, built the English way. It says I still do not study — a state that never started — where lam aʿud says a habit ended.

sentences.usage: Marking the end of something you used to do.
sentences.mnemonic: no longer = did not go back: lam aʿud, then the old habit.

sentences.display: aṣbaḥa al-jaww bārid fī tilka al-ayyām
sentences.script: أصبح الجو بارد في تلك الأيام
sentences.cue: The weather turned cold in those days
sentences.literal: Became the-weather cold in those the-days

words.note: A third sister. It takes a predicate rather than a verb — an adjective or a noun — and reports a change into that state.
The far demonstrative for a feminine word or a non-human plural. tilka al-ayyām, those days, is the phrase this module lives in.

sentences.trap: English became needs a subject in front of it. Arabic puts the sister verb FIRST and the subject after, so the sentence opens on the change itself.
sentences.sound: aṣ-BA-ḥa: the ṣ is heavy and pulls the vowel after it back, and the final ḥ is the breathy throat one.

variations.display: aṣbaḥa al-ʿamal ṣaʿb fī tilka al-ayyām
variations.script: أصبح العمل صعب في تلك الأيام
variations.cue: The work turned hard in those days
variations.changed: what changed, and into what

variations.display: ṣāra al-jaww bārid fī tilka al-ayyām
variations.script: صار الجو بارد في تلك الأيام
variations.cue: The weather turned cold in those days
variations.changed: ṣāra for aṣbaḥa — the two are near enough to swap here

mistake.why: Two sisters stacked. Each one already carries the whole frame, so one is always enough; stacking them is the commonest over-reach once the class is named.

sentences.usage: Setting the scene of a past stretch of time.
sentences.mnemonic: aṣbaḥa = it got to be, and what it got to be comes last.

sentences.cue: The work became hard after that

words.note: The fourth sister, and aṣbaḥa's everyday twin. aṣbaḥa leans on a change that has settled; ṣāra is the plainer word for the same move.

sentences.trap: English has become, get, turn and go for this, and picks by collocation. Arabic has two words that cover the lot, and neither one is tied to a particular adjective.
sentences.sound: ṢĀ-ra: one long heavy syllable, the ṣ made with the tongue flat and the back of the mouth open.

variations.display: ṣārat al-madrasa kabīra baʿda dhālika
variations.script: صارت المدرسة كبيرة بعد ذلك
variations.cue: The school became big after that
variations.changed: a feminine subject, so the sister takes -at and the adjective agrees

variations.display: aṣbaḥa al-ʿamal ṣaʿb baʿda dhālika
variations.script: أصبح العمل صعب بعد ذلك
variations.cue: The work became hard after that
variations.changed: aṣbaḥa for ṣāra — the swap runs both ways

mistake.why: kāna behind another sister. The sisters are alternatives to one another, never a chain: whichever one is at the head of the sentence has already done the whole job.

sentences.usage: Naming the moment a state changed.
sentences.mnemonic: ṣāra and aṣbaḥa are one word with two spellings, near enough.

sentences.display: fī al-māḍī kuntu adrus kull yawm, ammā al-ān fa-adhhab ilā al-ʿamal
sentences.script: في الماضي كنت أدرس كل يوم، أما الآن فأذهب إلى العمل
sentences.cue: In the past I used to study every day, but now I go to work
sentences.literal: In the-past I-was I-study every day, as-for the-now so-I-go to the-work

words.note: The phrase that opens a then-against-now contrast. It is indexed whole, and it sets up the ammā clause rather than standing alone.

sentences.trap: English can leave the contrast implied — I used to study; now I work. Arabic marks BOTH halves, and the second half's fa- is not optional once ammā has opened it.
sentences.sound: fī al-MĀ-ḍī: the ḍ is heavy and the ī after it is long, so the word ends on a low falling note.

variations.display: fī al-māḍī kāna yadrus, ammā al-ān fa-yadhhab ilā al-ʿamal
variations.script: في الماضي كان يدرس، أما الآن فيذهب إلى العمل
variations.cue: In the past he used to study, but now he goes to work
variations.changed: the person, carried through both halves

variations.display: al-māḍī jamīl, ammā al-ān fa-adhhab ilā al-ʿamal kull yawm
variations.script: الماضي جميل، أما الآن فأذهب إلى العمل كل يوم
variations.cue: The past is beautiful, but now I go to work every day
variations.changed: al-māḍī standing on its own as a noun, with no fī in front

mistake.display: fī al-māḍī kuntu adrus, ammā al-ān adhhab ilā al-ʿamal
mistake.script: في الماضي كنت أدرس، أما الآن أذهب إلى العمل
mistake.why: ammā with no fa- behind it. L4-M2 opened the pair and it is a pair: ammā raises the topic and fa- answers it, and the answer cannot arrive bare.

sentences.usage: Setting a life you had against the life you have, in one breath.
sentences.mnemonic: ammā asks, fa- answers; kāna is on one side of the comma only.

words.note: Formerly. It carries the -an ending of L1-M4's dāʾiman and aḥyānan, and it points at a stretch that is over.
Small — the opposite of L1-M3's kabīr, and it agrees with its noun the same way.

sentences.trap: English previously can sit anywhere in the sentence. Arabic puts it at the front, and the verb still comes before the subject behind it.
sentences.sound: SĀ-bi-qan: the q is made far back against the soft palate, deeper than an English k.

variations.display: sābiqan kānat al-madrasa ṣaghīra
variations.script: سابقاً كانت المدرسة صغيرة
variations.cue: Previously the school was small
variations.changed: a feminine subject, so both kāna and the adjective agree with it

variations.display: kāna al-bayt ṣaghīr fī tilka al-ayyām
variations.script: كان البيت صغير في تلك الأيام
variations.cue: The house was small in those days
variations.changed: the time phrase moved to the end, as tilka al-ayyām

mistake.why: A nominal sentence with no kāna. Arabic's verbless sentence is PRESENT by default, so this says the house is small now — and sābiqan cannot drag it into the past on its own.

sentences.usage: Comparing how a place used to be with how it is.
sentences.mnemonic: sābiqan sets the time; kāna is still what carries the past.

sentences.cue: In childhood I was a happy child

words.note: Childhood, as a stretch of time. The article assimilates to the ṭ, so it is written aṭ-ṭ- and heard as one long ṭ.
A child, younger than L2-M3's walad. Its feminine is ṭifla.

sentences.trap: English says as a child and needs no verb. Arabic needs kāna: without it the sentence slides into the present and claims you are a child now.
sentences.sound: aṭ-ṭu-FŪ-la: the doubled ṭ at the front is held, and the ū in the middle is long.

variations.display: fī aṭ-ṭufūla kuntu ṭifla saʿīda
variations.script: في الطفولة كنت طفلة سعيدة
variations.cue: In childhood I was a happy child (a girl speaking)
variations.changed: the speaker's gender, on both the noun and the adjective

variations.display: fī aṭ-ṭufūla kuntu adrus fī tilka al-madrasa
variations.script: في الطفولة كنت أدرس في تلك المدرسة
variations.cue: In childhood I used to study at that school
variations.changed: a habit instead of a state, so the frame goes back to kāna + present

mistake.why: anā where kuntu belongs. The pronoun makes a present nominal sentence; only kāna puts it in the past.

sentences.usage: Reaching back past the years you can date.

sentences.cue: The manager is still at the office

words.note: mā zāla's present-shaped twin, and the commoner one in writing. Same sister, same slot, and here with a predicate rather than a verb behind it.

sentences.trap: English still is one word whatever the tense. Arabic has a past-shaped mā zāla and a present-shaped lā yazāl for the same idea, and neither is about time — both mean now.
sentences.sound: lā ya-ZĀL: the negative lā is long, and yazāl carries the stress on its long ā.

variations.display: mā zāla al-mudīr fī al-maktab
variations.script: ما زال المدير في المكتب
variations.cue: The manager is still at the office
variations.changed: mā zāla for lā yazāl — the same claim in the past-shaped twin

variations.display: lā yazāl al-maktab maftūḥ
variations.script: لا يزال المكتب مفتوح
variations.cue: The office is still open
variations.changed: the predicate: L3-M8's participle instead of a place

mistake.why: lam put on zāla. The family's negative is lam yaʿud, no longer; lā yazāl is already a negative on the inside and takes nothing more.

sentences.usage: Reporting that a state has not ended.
sentences.mnemonic: lā yazāl and mā zāla: two shapes, one now.

sentences.display: kuntu ṭālib sābiqan, wa al-ān aṣbaḥtu mudīr
sentences.script: كنت طالب سابقاً، والآن أصبحت مدير
sentences.cue: I was a student previously, and now I have become a manager
sentences.literal: I-was student previously, and the-now I-became manager

words.note: The I-cell of S04's aṣbaḥa. The sisters take the same person endings as any past verb, so kuntu and aṣbaḥtu rhyme.

sentences.trap: English marks the change with a perfect — I have become — and Arabic marks it with a plain past. Nothing in aṣbaḥtu says recently; al-ān does that.
sentences.sound: aṣ-BAḤ-tu: the ḥ before the -tu is the breathy throat one and is not swallowed.

variations.display: kuntu ṭālib sābiqan, wa al-ān aṣbaḥtu muwaẓẓaf
variations.script: كنت طالب سابقاً، والآن أصبحت موظف
variations.cue: I was a student previously, and now I have become a clerk
variations.changed: what you became

variations.display: kāna ṭālib sābiqan, wa al-ān aṣbaḥa mudīr
variations.script: كان طالب سابقاً، والآن أصبح مدير
variations.cue: He was a student previously, and now he has become a manager
variations.changed: the person, carried across both halves

mistake.display: kuntu ṭālib sābiqan, wa al-ān kuntu mudīr
mistake.script: كنت طالب سابقاً، والآن كنت مدير
mistake.why: kāna in the now half. kāna is the past sister; the one that reaches the present from a change is aṣbaḥa, and al-ān cannot repair the wrong verb.

sentences.usage: The one-line version of your own history.
sentences.mnemonic: kuntu then, aṣbaḥtu now — the sisters carry the whole story.
